# telemetryd

> A single-binary observability backend. OTLP in; the Loki, Tempo and Prometheus query
> APIs out. One process, one port, one data directory, no sidecars and no collector.
> Written in Rust, MIT licensed, at github.com/cboxdk/telemetryd.

Run it with `telemetryd serve` and no arguments. It listens on `127.0.0.1:4319`, stores
data beside itself, keeps 7 days of logs and traces and 30 days of metrics, and stays
under a 10 GiB disk budget. Every setting is also an environment variable named
`TELEMETRYD_<SECTION>_<KEY>`; precedence is defaults, then `telemetryd.toml`, then the
environment, then CLI flags.

`GET /` needs no token. With `Accept: application/json` it returns an identity document —
`product` (always `"telemetryd"`), `version`, `storage_format_version`, `signals`, and
`surfaces[].auth` naming the credential each group of routes wants. With `text/html` it
is a page; otherwise plain text. Use it to confirm what is listening at an address before
you hold a credential for it.

`GET /status` needs no token either, and answers the same four identity fields to a
caller that has none. Send the admin token to the same path and you get the deployment
picture instead — unchanged from what it always returned. Both are `200`: tell them
apart by the absence of `storage`, not by the status code. The identity response carries
`Cache-Control: no-store` and `Vary: Authorization`, because one URL with two bodies
chosen by a request header must not be cached by anything shared.

Both describe the product, never the deployment: no app names, no counts, no disk
figures, no retention, no listen address, no relay configuration, no per-surface auth
state. Those need the admin token. Publishing the version to an unauthenticated caller
is deliberate and is not configurable; the reasoning is in the configuration reference.
A `401` is also an identification rather than silence — every one carries
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="telemetryd"`.

## The thing most likely to mislead you

telemetryd serves the Loki, Tempo and Prometheus **APIs**, not those products. The
supported query surface is derived from what its client actually calls, so it is a
deliberate subset — writing a valid PromQL or LogQL expression is not enough for it to
run here.

Anything outside the subset is refused with HTTP 400 and a structured body naming the
construct: `{"error":{"code":"unsupported_feature","feature":"PromQL function `topk`"}}`.
The languages are parsed in full and then lowered, which is why the error can name the
function rather than reporting a syntax error.

Verified against a running instance:

- **PromQL works** for selectors and label matchers, `rate`, `increase`,
  `histogram_quantile`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`, `by (...)`, `without (...)`,
  `offset`, and arithmetic on a series.
- **PromQL is refused** for `topk`, `bottomk`, `quantile`, `stddev`, `irate`, `delta`,
  `absent`, and comparison operators such as `> 5`.
- **LogQL works** for stream selectors, `|=`, `!=`, `|~`, `| json` and `| logfmt`.
- **LogQL is refused** for `| line_format` and for every metric query over log streams —
  `rate`, `count_over_time`, `sum`. Use the Prometheus API for pre-aggregated metrics.
- **TraceQL works** for `{}`, attribute equality, `duration > 100ms`, `status = error`,
  `name = "..."`, and `&&` between conditions.
- **TraceQL is refused** for `||` between conditions and for `| count() > 2`.

One request does not return everything. `GET /loki/api/v1/query_range` clamps `limit`
to 5,000 and `GET /api/search` clamps it to 1,000 — **silently**, so asking for a
million and receiving five thousand is the cap, not missing data. Page by advancing
`start` past the newest record you received, or use `GET /api/v1/export`, which returns
up to 200,000 records per request. The Prometheus range endpoint is the exception and
refuses loudly: more than 11,000 points per series is a `400` telling you to widen
`step`.

Prefer a narrow time range on any query with a substring filter. A term that appears
nowhere is skipped without reading a segment; a term whose trigrams are individually
common — a numeric order id, say — cannot be, and the time bound is what saves the scan.

## Sending data

OTLP over HTTP in **either encoding** — JSON or protobuf. The `Content-Type` picks the
parser and changes nothing else. There is no gRPC endpoint.

- `POST /v1/logs`, `POST /v1/traces`, `POST /v1/metrics` — OTLP/HTTP, JSON or protobuf
- `POST /api/v1/write` — Prometheus `remote_write` (snappy + protobuf)

`gzip`, `deflate` and `zstd` request bodies are decompressed. Records are rejected
individually and the reason is reported in OTLP's `partialSuccess` field, so a `200`
does not mean everything was stored — read the body.

The resource attribute `service.name` becomes the `app` label and severity becomes
`level`. Every other attribute is stored but is not a stream label unless listed in
`ingest.stream_labels`, which is the cardinality contract. A resource attribute no label
claimed — `k8s.pod.name`, `host.name`, `cloud.region` — is kept as a record attribute
under the spelling you sent, so it is queryable and it survives export. A record
attribute of the same name wins; a promoted one is not stored twice.

A stock OpenTelemetry SDK works with no configuration: the default
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf` is served, and so is `http/json`.

`GET /debug` is a server-rendered page for the question "is my data arriving": the last
100 records per signal, tabs for logs, traces and metrics, and a query box with
suggestions built from this instance's own labels. Meant to be opened in a browser against
a real deployment — an instance with tokens shows a sign-in form and takes the admin token
(or the query token when no admin token is set), holding it in an `HttpOnly` cookie;
an instance without tokens is open. `Authorization: Bearer` works too, for scripts.

## Authentication

Three independent tokens guard three surfaces: `auth.ingest_token` for writes,
`auth.query_token` for the read APIs, `auth.admin_token` for `/status` and `/metrics`.
Send them as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. OIDC access tokens are accepted alongside
them when `auth.oidc.issuer` is set; scopes are not a hierarchy, so an admin scope does
not grant reads.

telemetryd refuses to start when bound to a non-loopback address with no token
configured. That is deliberate and should not be worked around with `--insecure`.

## Docs

- [Quickstart](https://cbox.dk/packages/telemetryd/docs/quickstart): install, run, send, query — in one read
- [Installation](https://cbox.dk/packages/telemetryd/docs/getting-started/installation): includes a copy-paste brief for an agent
- [Sending data](https://cbox.dk/packages/telemetryd/docs/getting-started/sending-data): endpoints, labels, and what a 200 does not mean
- [Docker](https://cbox.dk/packages/telemetryd/docs/getting-started/docker): the container, and the tokens it generates on first start
- [Configuration reference](https://cbox.dk/packages/telemetryd/docs/configuration/reference): every option with its default
- [COMPATIBILITY.md](https://github.com/cboxdk/telemetryd/blob/main/COMPATIBILITY.md): the authoritative API subset, endpoint by endpoint
- [BUILD-STATUS.md](https://github.com/cboxdk/telemetryd/blob/main/BUILD-STATUS.md): what is built, what is not, and what is deliberately absent
- [Cookbook](https://cbox.dk/packages/telemetryd/docs/cookbook/_index): task-shaped recipes — relay mode, single sign-on, export and import, exposing it safely

## Do not

- Do not add an OpenTelemetry Collector. Applications send OTLP straight to telemetryd.
- Do not reach for a gRPC OTLP exporter; only the HTTP endpoints exist. Either HTTP
  encoding is fine.
- Do not assume an unsupported query construct is a bug. Read the `feature` field.
- Do not publish port 4319 to the internet in plain HTTP. Terminate TLS in front, or set
  `server.tls.cert_file` and `key_file`.
